U.S. Tariffs on Bulgarian Electric Utilities Products Put Industry Under Strain

Sofia—The Bulgarian electric utilities industry is facing mounting pressure after the United States imposed a 25% tariff on imports of electricity transmission equipment and related products originating from Bulgaria. The measure, which went into effect earlier this month, has already begun to impact producers, including the state-owned Bulgarian Energy Holding EAD, and is reverberating through the sector.

The U.S. Trade Representative’s office cited concerns over “unfair competitive practices” and “market access barriers” as reasons for the new tariffs, but Bulgarian officials and industry leaders have pushed back, calling the move “unjustified” and warning of significant economic consequences.

Early estimates from the Bulgarian Association of Electric Utilities indicate exports of transformers, switchgear, and smart grid components to the United States have dropped by nearly 40% since the tariffs were enacted. “Our members have seen orders postponed or cancelled, and some shipments are stuck at U.S. ports awaiting clarification,” said Veselin Petrov, spokesperson for the association. “This is already affecting revenue, cash flow, and future investment plans.”

Bulgarian Energy Holding EAD, a major exporter of high-voltage transmission equipment, confirmed it is experiencing delays in fulfilling U.S. contracts. “Our long-term agreements with American partners are now in jeopardy,” a company representative stated. “We are working closely with Bulgarian and U.S. authorities to seek a resolution, but the uncertainty is hurting our competitiveness.”

Analysts note that Bulgarian firms invested heavily in recent years to expand production and comply with international standards, with the United States representing one of their fastest-growing export markets. “The timing couldn’t be worse,” said Milena Ivanova, an energy sector analyst at Sofia-based consultancy Balkan Insight Partners. “The industry is already navigating high inflation and supply chain challenges. An abrupt drop in export demand could force companies to cut back on output or delay planned expansions.”

Trade unions have raised concerns about job security. “Workers in our sector are worried about potential layoffs if the situation drags on,” said Dimitar Kolev, leader of the Electric Utilities Workers’ Union. “We urge both governments to return to the negotiating table.”

As talks between Bulgarian and U.S. officials continue, industry leaders are calling for swift action to prevent long-term damage to one of Bulgaria’s strategically important export sectors.
